title: The storage callback ABI crosses compiler conventions
method: Exact-build call-site inspection; ARM and Thumb receivers; negative control
observation: The measured completion convention splits its final 64-bit count between a register and the stack. The contemporary bare-metal EABI comparison places it differently. Synthetic receivers verify both words and register preservation; the ordinary-EABI control fails as expected.
limits: The probe isolates the boundary. It does not recover the full Darwin C++ ABI or exercise a physical storage device.

excerpts.content: The embedded `IOBlockStorageDriver` calls the provider's legacy 64-bit asynchronous read/write slot with block in `r2/r3`, count in the first two stack words, and the three completion fields by value after it. Its completion helper invokes the action with target in `r0`, parameter in `r1`, status in `r2`, byte-count low word in `r3` and high word at the top of the stack. A normal EABI call with a 64-bit fourth argument places both words on the stack instead. The mismatch would corrupt a transfer's completion count even if its sector data were correct.

title: Synchronous completion grows the kernel stack
method: Per-request trace and deferred-completion control
observation: Inline completion reentered the provider while earlier frames remained on the kernel stack. Deferring completion through an existing kernel thread-call mechanism allowed the unchanged one-sector diagnostic to finish 39 reads.
limits: This early read-only diagnostic had one pending slot and does not validate the later writable queue under saturation.

records.access: Private project record; original material is not distributed

exhibits.title: Same one-sector limit; different completion lifetime
rows: While earlier frames remain on the stack
exhibits.interpretation: Increasing transfer size would hide the recursion depth. Deferral changes the lifetime of the stack frames while preserving the one-sector diagnostic.

excerpts.content:
The first implementation completed reads synchronously. It read sectors 0–16 correctly, but the driver's next-chunk callback reentered the provider before prior frames unwound. The next request faulted at the kernel-stack boundary. Increasing transfer size would only change the depth, so the adapter instead queues successful completions on one preallocated XNU thread call. Each worker snapshots callback arguments before releasing the pending slot. Reentrant requests can queue the next callback without retaining the previous transfer stack.

[…]

The unchanged one-sector request limit then completed 39 reads with no panic or Undefined Instruction exception. The 98 previously observed page-stepping Data Aborts remained; their cause is still unresolved.

title: Two consecutive physical storage gates passed
method: Matched 720-second runs; clean guest reboot; full recovery copies before host attachment
observation: After the storage backpressure and restart integration corrections, two consecutive phone boots returned to recovery automatically. Both full data copies passed read-only fsck with a clean bit; root hashes were unchanged.
limits: Both runs recorded zero overflow-path uses. These results do not validate queue saturation, arbitrary power loss or application-setting persistence.

exhibits.title: The two physical acceptance runs
exhibits.interpretation: Both data copies were taken before USB host attachment. Clean storage acceptance and battery loss are simultaneous findings; the latter is not erased by the successful filesystem check. Neither run exercised queue overflow.

exhibits.title: Identities retained for the integrity comparison
exhibits.interpretation: The data digest identifies the examined output; data is expected to change. The root equality is the separate write-containment observation.

excerpts.content:
The first corrected 720-second phone run reached `BOOT_TIME` at 34 seconds,
printed 37 heartbeats with rising idle/WFI counters, and recorded zero queue
waits, overflow uses, failed request starts, CMD17/CMD24 failures, or error
completions. The BSD reboot callback fired at 728 seconds, `MACH Reboot`
followed at 731 seconds, and the phone returned to Jumpdrive through WDOG0
without a manual reset. A full data copy through Jumpdrive UART before USB
host attach had its clean bit set and passed read-only fsck (exit 0); the
root hash remained
`a2a4776df7602d41cd6e83e7b873ae4cfc0db30cff87303b6d608e520c01e17c`.
Battery changed from 31% / 3.754 V before boot to 27% / 3.740 V after
recovery, when Jumpdrive again reported charging. This is one of the two
required consecutive clean runs. Its full data copy is the rollback for the
second run.

[…]

The second consecutive 720-second phone run used the same staged kernel,
storage, and timer hashes, with the first run's fsck-clean data volume left
in place. The battery read 34% / 3.830 V and Charging in Jumpdrive at the
restored 500 mA USB input limit before boot. It reached `BOOT_TIME` at about
70 seconds, printed 37 heartbeats with rising idle/WFI counters, and had no
queue waits, overflow uses, failed request starts, CMD17/CMD24 failures,
drain failures, or error completions. The BSD reboot callback fired at 728
seconds and the phone returned to Jumpdrive through WDOG0 at 731 seconds.
The full 512 MiB data copy taken through Jumpdrive UART before USB host
attach has SHA-256

exhibits.title: Exact byte identity and header state
rows: Root hash during each guest run
exhibits.interpretation: Bit 0x100 records clean unmount in these observed headers. The clean-shutdown control and the later host stop produce distinguishable volume states despite fsck exit 0.

excerpts.content:
A follow-up removed the two pre-existing data-volume fsck warnings on an
**offline, disposable data copy**. `fsck_hfs -dfy` changed only data-volume
sectors 2, 98384 and 1048574; the catalog-sector changes set the two
`HasFolderCount` flags. Read-only `fsck_hfs -dfn` then exited 0. No root
image, phone partition or backup was repaired. The same QEMU partition-level
root read-only patch and data-only storage guard booted this repaired input.
The first guest wrote the exact 47-byte `START`/`OK` marker, returned zero
from `sync(2)`, and reset via the guest watchdog without QMP at 15.5 seconds.
The root hash remained unchanged, and data fsck exited 0 after the reset.

A fresh QEMU process then used that data with the readback-job root. It
created a 47-byte readback file whose bytes exactly match both the persisted
marker and the original guest output. Its root hash remained unchanged, and
data fsck again exited 0, including the bitmap, catalog and volume-header
checks. This second run did **not** print `BOOT_TIME` during its 50-second
window, although it mounted both volumes and completed the readback job; the
prior pair reached `BOOT_TIME` with the same readback root and an unrepaired
data input. The clean-data pair therefore proves QEMU data write, sync,
guest reboot and fresh-process readback with fsck exit 0, but not a reliable
second normal boot or physical durability.

[…]

The same job on a fresh card with the watchdog-enabled kernel caused QEMU to
exit on the guest's request after 51.01 seconds, without a QMP or host reset.
The data header retained its clean-unmount bit (`0x80000100`), full read-only
fsck exited 0, and both the original marker and guest readback contained the
same 47 bytes (SHA-256
`4f319ed2db04f95950946175d8b4736c254db39fcbddb3a5c985d23f977a5853`).
The root partition hash did not change during the guest run. A third fresh
QEMU process, using that card's data and the original readback root, mounted
data and reached `BOOT_TIME` at 77.83 seconds. Its root also stayed unchanged
and data fsck exited 0. That third process was stopped by the host at 90
seconds, leaving the data clean-unmount bit clear again (`0x80000000`). Thus
guest sync/readback/watchdog reboot produced a clean HFS volume that booted
again; a host stop still leaves the older guest's next mount vulnerable to
the dirty-header failure above. These runs touched no physical phone media.

| Region | Half-open physical range | Ownership |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modeled RAM | `0x40000000–0x60000000` | QEMU's 512 MiB RAM |
| XNU advertised memory | `0x50000000–0x57400000` | Includes staged kernel; first-free boundary is `0x506c0000` |

[…]

The previous adapter used scanout RAM as the default CoreSurface backing.
Copying another surface into scanout therefore overwrote the default source,
and returning to the default surface skipped copying. The source now requires
a distinct, page-aligned default allocation with validated nonoverlapping
32-bit ranges, and copies every selected non-null surface. A host regression
executes setup and A → B → A presentation, checking whole-frame equality and
unchanged default-source contents alongside one-shot console ownership.

exhibits.interpretation: The worker signals readiness after registration returns. The paired captures connect the blocked sensor registration to the startup wait without claiming a working replacement sensor or live input.

excerpts.content:
The main thread waits in HID session initialization during application
startup. The same worker whose kernel stack reaches AppleISL29003 has this
user call chain: HID session thread, service-set traversal, service
registration, ALS state setup, HID service open, IOKit connection method,
Mach message. Exact library analysis shows the worker signals readiness
only after these registration calls return. Its kernel-side sensor call
is blocked on a shared legacy IIC controller queue. Other kernel threads
also wait on that controller; this does not identify a sensor register
failure or prove that this particular transfer reached hardware.

[…]

After the same 90-second observation window:

- SpringBoard has seven threads, compared with five in the baseline.
- Its main thread has left the HID readiness wait and reached
  GraphicsServices' event loop inside UIKit application run.
- The HID worker has passed registration/signaling and reached its own
  CoreFoundation run loop.
- The unsupported AppleISL service is absent; the buttons HID client still
  attaches. Other legacy IIC clients are not established as working.
- Both observed run-loop threads wait for Mach messages, which is expected
  at an idle snapshot. This does not prove input delivery or responsiveness.
- Captured display pixels remain XNU verbose text. No native graphical
  session, touchscreen or app interaction is demonstrated.

title: Reboot acceptance extends beyond the printed message
method: Explicit UART request; observed recovery return; full data-volume check
observation: The corrected UART listener survived input, accepted the explicit request and returned through BSD shutdown to recovery. A later remote-only run passed the former three-minute cutoff, rebooted on request and passed full data fsck with an unchanged root.
limits: The command is a dedicated reboot channel, not a shell. It depends on a live polling path and does not guarantee recovery from arbitrary kernel failure.

records.access: Private project record; original material is not distributed

exhibits.title: A board mismatch at the same MMIO offset
rows: Not handled as the native UART source
exhibits.interpretation: A plausible driver name does not make the register layouts compatible. The first receive event exposed that mismatch.

exhibits.title: Progress beyond the printed acknowledgement
rows: Harmless RX survived; recovery about 6 s after request
Ten heartbeats past old cutoff; recovery about 6 s later
512 MiB; fsck exit 0; clean bit set
exhibits.interpretation: The record distinguishes the first interrupt-masking correction from the later explicit IER clear. Actual recovery and filesystem checks complete the reboot claim.

excerpts.content:
The phone Apple tree originally exposed `uart0` at the real A64 UART0 MMIO
address `0x01c28000` as `uart,s5l8900x`. AppleS5L8900XSerial attached in the
first physical UART-command trial. Its Samsung UCON register at offset 4
overlaps A64 UART IER. The first trial stopped printing after host RX and did
not reach either command acknowledgement or the five-minute fallback. The
live A64 UART0 interrupt is GIC SPI 32.

[…]

The corrected five-minute physical gate captured
`spi32_before=00000001 after=00000000 ier=00000001`: masking was actually
needed on the phone. A harmless RX byte did not stop the idle or UART
heartbeats. The full token was accepted, `MACH Reboot` appeared, and
Jumpdrive returned six seconds after the host request. The subsequent full
512 MiB data copy had its HFS clean bit set and passed `fsck_hfs -dfn` with
exit 0; the root partition SHA-256 remained
`a2a4776df7602d41cd6e83e7b873ae4cfc0db30cff87303b6d608e520c01e17c`.
UART0 IER still read 1 in that gate because U-Boot had left it enabled.

[…]

Its first phone
run logged `spi32_before=00000001 after=00000000 ier=00000000` at listener
startup. Ten subsequent UART heartbeats retained `ier=00000000 spi32=0
remask=0` beyond the old three-minute cutoff. The host requested a reboot,
and Jumpdrive returned about six seconds later. Its complete post-run data
copy had the clean bit set and passed fsck with exit 0; the root hash was
unchanged.

title: Zero-valued MMIO can fabricate device presence
method: Mixed-board restore-stage observation and source/disassembly comparison
observation: A phone restore-stage diagnostic running on the iPod QEMU model reported a radio board in a model without a radio. The relevant input defaulted to zero, which the diagnostic interpreted as presence.
limits: This is a false positive about a detection predicate, not evidence of a working modem or a complete iPhone profile.

records.access: Private project record; original material is not distributed

exhibits.title: A specific address explains the false detection
exhibits.interpretation: The zero value satisfies the firmware’s presence predicate. The QEMU model has no radio; the observation demonstrates a false positive in the model contract.

exhibits.title: Interpret the predicate, not the message
exhibits.interpretation: The nonzero row describes the inspected branch, not an executed negative-control run. Explicitly separating those evidence types prevents a second unsupported claim.

excerpts.content:
The read helper selects GPIO bank 7, bit 1: it reads a word at `0x3e400004 + 7 * 0x20 = 0x3e4000e4` and tests mask `0x2`. A zero result takes the branch to the radio-present message at `0x18000ed4`; a nonzero result prints that no radio board was detected.

[…]

The pinned QEMU `hw/arm/ipod_touch_gpio.c` handles only offset `0x2c4` in its read callback and returns zero for every other GPIO offset. Its write callback ignores all writes. Thus the read at offset `0xe4` supplies the low bit value that this iBEC interprets as an installed radio board. This explains the existing console observation without implying a working baseband.

Run 048 sent values within 0–32,767; the guest read touch start, move, end and full-end frames, and the captured screen changed from the dialog to the full SpringBoard icon grid. The touchscreen's Y-velocity calculation also now uses the Y displacement. These results establish one working tap, not keyboard editing or all gestures.

[…]

Run 051 reached the dialog and dismissed it by touch, with 800 accepted 3D renders, zero 3D or 2D rejections, zero graphics recovery messages and no panic through 73 seconds. This is a bounded observation; longer uptime remains to be checked.

[…]

The user's subsequent visible 4A102 session reached Settings, Calculator, Safari's keyboard and Notes, with changing degrees of responsiveness and visual artifacts. In the final recorded run, Notes reached a pending 2D graphics hang, then QEMU aborted when an idle zero byte reached the multitouch SPI command decoder. These are two distinct failures; the graphics hang remains unexplained.
